blocks.content: A container that will not start at all has a smaller, more specific set of usual causes than one that starts and then crashes, this topic walks through a systematic way to triage it.

Rather than guessing, work through this in order: docker ps -a to see the exit status, docker logs to see what the application itself said before exiting, and docker inspect to check the full configuration actually being used, this order almost always surfaces the real cause quickly.

blocks.alt: A consistent order that almost always finds the cause quickly

blocks.content: 2. A Typo in CMD or ENTRYPOINT
blocks.text: 2. A Typo in CMD or ENTRYPOINT

blocks.content: If the command specified simply does not exist, or is misspelled, the container exits immediately, usually with exit code 127, covered in the Exit Codes topic, docker logs typically shows a shell-level "command not found" style error directly.

blocks.alt: An immediate exit, with a command-not-found style error in the logs

blocks.content: 3. A Host Port Already in Use
blocks.text: 3. A Host Port Already in Use

blocks.content: As covered in the Networking Issues topic, trying to publish a port that is already bound to something else on the host causes the container to fail outright at start time, with a clear "port is already allocated" error.

blocks.alt: The container never gets a chance to start at all

blocks.content: 4. A Required Environment Variable Is Missing
blocks.text: 4. A Required Environment Variable Is Missing

blocks.content: An application that expects a specific environment variable (a database URL, an API key) and fails fast when it is absent will crash immediately on start, docker logs should show the application's own error message about the missing configuration.

blocks.alt: The app itself refuses to start without required configuration

blocks.content: Running an image built for one CPU architecture (say, x86_64) on a host of a different architecture (an ARM-based Apple Silicon Mac or an ARM cloud instance) produces a distinctive exec format error, the fix is pulling or building an image for the correct architecture, or using a multi-platform image.

blocks.alt: A distinctive error that immediately points at an architecture mismatch

blocks.content:
docker run --rm myimage
# standard_init_linux.go:228: exec user process caused: exec format error
# This specific message means an architecture mismatch, not an app bug.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A container that will not start at all should be triaged in order: ps -a for exit status, logs for the actual error, inspect for full configuration.
A handful of specific causes cover most cases: a bad command, a port conflict, missing required configuration, or a CPU architecture mismatch.
